claims.text: A rollout is triggered only by a .spec.template change; the Deployment moves Pods to a ReplicaSet for that template: a new one (own pod-template-hash) unless an old ReplicaSet has exactly that template. Scaling does not.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Deployments (Updating a Deployment; note on rollout triggers)

claims.text: The default Deployment strategy is RollingUpdate: the new ReplicaSet is scaled up while the old one is scaled down, so Pods of both versions run at the same time.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Deployments (Strategy: Rolling Update Deployment; default)

claims.text: maxSurge and maxUnavailable both default to 25%; maxSurge limits Pods created above desired, maxUnavailable limits Pods unavailable below desired during the update.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Deployments (Max Unavailable; Max Surge: default value is 25%)

claims.text: For replicas: 2 with defaults, the Deployment allows at most 3 Pods (one extra) and none unavailable, moving one Pod at a time: old 2/new 1, old 1/new 1, old 1/new 2, old 0/new 2.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Deployments (maxSurge rounded up, maxUnavailable rounded down); outputs rolling-update.txt (most wanted 3)

claims.text: kubectl apply returns once the API server stores the change; kubectl rollout status waits until the rollout has finished ('successfully rolled out').
After the rollout, the old ReplicaSet is kept with 0 replicas (it is not deleted).
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Deployments (old ReplicaSets scaled to 0; revisionHistoryLimit); outputs rolling-update.txt

claims.text: Without a readiness probe (and minReadySeconds 0), a Pod is counted available as soon as its container is running/Ready, so the rollout proceeds even if the app cannot yet serve requests.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Pod lifecycle (container probes: readiness default Success); Deployments (minReadySeconds)

claims.text: deploy/k8s/lessons/api-deployment-1.0.0.yaml@stage-2 differs from api-deployment.yaml only in comments and image tag (1.0.0); no strategy section.
claims.source_hint: git -C examples/don-hang diff of the two files @ stage-2

claims.text: rolling-update.sh re-creates the Deployment from api-deployment.yaml, stores old_rs, applies 1.0.0, reads both ReplicaSets in a loop with a 0.2 s pause between reads, prints both-ready=yes and most wanted=3, rollout status, ReplicaSets sorted by replicas.
Re-applying a template identical to an old ReplicaSet's makes the Deployment scale that existing ReplicaSet back up instead of creating a new one.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Deployments (Rollover; existing ReplicaSet matching template is reused)

claims.text: kubectl get -w (--watch) keeps running and prints a line each time a listed object changes.
With minReadySeconds 0 and no readiness probe, a Pod is available as soon as it is ready; ReplicaSets created by a Deployment select on a pod-template-hash label holding the template hash.
kubectl get -o wide adds CONTAINERS, IMAGES and SELECTOR columns for ReplicaSets; --sort-by=.spec.replicas sorts rows by that field.
Right after kubectl apply returns 'configured', the ReplicaSet being replaced still has Pods for a few seconds (a 2-replica api rollout takes about 3 s here), visible with kubectl get replicasets -w.
claims.source_hint: executed by reviewer r2 (rv-ru2 from the lesson's manifests: rollout ~3.0 s)
